---
title: "A pitch is a sequence, not a single number"
subtitle: "A short guide to the events and measurements behind the charts"
---

Pitching summaries often reduce a delivery to a speed or a peak. Motion-capture
data lets us look at how measurements change across the recorded movement.
These events help orient the plots; the dataset does not label every point as
a universal phase of pitching.

## Three moments to keep in mind

1. **Foot plant (FP)** is the point when the stride foot contacts the ground.
   The dataset includes some body positions and angles at this event.
2. **Maximum external rotation (MER)** is a shoulder-position milestone in the
   dataset. The elbow flexion measure at MER describes one joint angle at that
   moment; it is not itself a measure of injury.
3. **Ball release (BR)** is the delivery endpoint represented in several
   pitch-level measures. The full-signal charts show values across the
   recorded timeline, rather than only at these named events.

## From movement to a chart

The [Explore page](explore.qmd) pairs shoulder internal/external rotation
velocity with elbow varus/valgus moment at matching timestamps. Its time-course
view then aligns trials by relative recorded duration. This makes the broad
shape of the measured signal easier to compare, but it does not mean every
pitch has identical timing or that a relative-time point corresponds exactly
to a named event above.

The [pitch comparison](compare.qmd) switches perspective: each point represents
one trial, using its pitch speed and peak elbow varus moment. Looking at both
views helps distinguish a changing signal within a pitch from differences
between pitches.

::: callout-note
An elbow moment is a biomechanical estimate of joint loading, not a direct
measurement of tissue damage. No injury outcomes are included in these data.
:::
